title: Haunted Wirral: Frightening UFO sightings
excerpt: Haunted Wirral: Tom Slemen explores alleged 1967 UFO sightings over Birkenhead and the July 17 1962 flying saucer mystery involving three missing vagrants in Wirral.
content:
WELCOME to Haunted Wirral, a feature series written by world-famous psychic researcher, Tom Slemen for the Globe.

RUMOURS have a peculiar way of springing up from nowhere, particularly those warning of some impending catastrophe, whether it be a deadly disease, an invasion by a foreign power or even an attack by visitors from another planet.

Someone in a New Brighton pub might make an extraordinary claim, which could be nothing more than an outrageous porky, yet before long, the same tall tale is being repeated in the waiting room of a doctor's surgery in Heswall.

And all this can happen without the assistance of mobile phones, social media or the internet.

In October 1967, long before the arrival of such technology, an alarming rumour swept across Wirral, Liverpool and Manchester.

According to the story, a mass landing of flying saucers was imminent and the Earth was about to receive some very unwelcome visitors.

The origins of this extraordinary scare may have been connected to what became known as the Great British Flying Saucer Hoax of 1967, which had taken place the previous month.

This elaborate practical joke had been devised by engineering apprentices from the Royal Aircraft Establishment at Farnborough, who hoped to raise money for charity.

The students constructed a number of convincing flying saucers from moulded fibreglass. Each measured approximately three feet across and 20 inches deep and contained an inexpensive battery-operated device that emitted mysterious electronic sounds.

Under cover of darkness, the apprentices deposited their creations at various locations across Britain, particularly in fields and other rural areas.

The discovery of these strange, bleeping objects initially caused considerable excitement. Even some police officers were reportedly taken in by the deception, while the Army went so far as to blow up some of the supposed extra-terrestrial machines.

Not long afterwards, reports emerged of mysterious luminous crosses appearing in the night skies over various parts of Britain, from Kent to Wirral.

These sightings did not appear to be connected with the students' hoax, although the astronomer Patrick Moore suggested that at least some of the strange aerial phenomena could be explained by people mistaking the exceptionally bright planet Venus for something more mysterious.

Many years later, I discussed several UFO encounters from the 1960s during an afternoon broadcast on BBC Radio Merseyside. The response was extraordinary, and the station's telephone switchboard was inundated with calls from listeners eager to share their own experiences.

One of the most intriguing accounts concerned an enormous, white, double-convex craft, resembling the classic flying saucer, which was reportedly witnessed by numerous people in the vicinity of Grange Road in Birkenhead, on a Saturday morning in late October 1967.

A listener named David told me that he had been making his way to the bank that morning, carrying several hundred pounds in takings from the shop where he worked.

As he walked along Grange Road, a smartly dressed, rather well-to-do woman suddenly tapped him on the shoulder.

David turned sharply, startled by the unexpected contact, particularly as he was carrying such a substantial amount of money.

The woman pointed towards the sky. 'Look at that,' she said. 'A flying saucer!'

David followed the direction of her outstretched finger and was astonished by what he saw.

Suspended high above the street was an enormous, flattened, metallic disc, with a shallow dome rising from its upper surface.

Its dull, silvery-grey exterior was covered with peculiar rectangular panels, dark markings and patches of discolouration that gave the impression of a machine which had travelled unimaginable distances.

There were no wings, propellers, exhausts or any other recognisable means of propulsion. Nevertheless, the gigantic object remained perfectly motionless in the unusually clear blue sky.

What disturbed David most, however, was something protruding from the centre of the craft's underside.

It resembled a long, black, mechanical serpent, composed of numerous flexible, ribbed sections. The appendage curved downwards like the neck of some monstrous snake, its narrow tip directed towards the people in the street below.

As David watched, the sinister-looking instrument began to move.

It turned slowly from side to side, almost as though it were examining the pedestrians, studying their movements and searching for some particular individual.

There was something deeply unnerving about this strange mechanical probe. It gave David the impression that the object was not simply passing over Birkenhead but was deliberately observing its inhabitants.

The craft itself remained utterly silent, and its serpentine appendage continued its peculiar movements, like an inquisitive mechanical eye surveying an unfamiliar world.

'What the hell is that?' David exclaimed.

By now, other people had noticed the extraordinary visitor.

Traffic along Grange Road and the surrounding streets was slowing to a crawl, and some motorists had brought their vehicles to a complete standstill. Pedestrians were staring upwards, pointing at the enormous saucer and exchanging bewildered remarks.

David could scarcely believe what he was witnessing.

Then he remembered the money he was carrying.

He had been told that the bank would close at half-past eleven, and he glanced anxiously at his wristwatch to make sure he still had sufficient time to deposit the shop's takings.

It was a momentary distraction, lasting no more than a few seconds, but when David raised his eyes towards the sky again, the flying saucer had disappeared.

He looked about in astonishment.

The well-dressed woman who had first drawn his attention to the object was still standing nearby, and David asked her what had happened.

She explained that the snake-like instrument had suddenly retracted into the underside of the craft. Then, without making a sound or moving away in any discernible direction, the enormous saucer had simply vanished into thin air.

David could hardly comprehend what she was telling him.

Gradually, the traffic began moving again, although several small groups of pedestrians remained on the pavements, discussing the extraordinary aerial visitation they had just witnessed.

Later that day, David returned home and excitedly told his father about the flying saucer.

His father was thoroughly unimpressed.

He dismissed the entire account, insisting that David must have imagined the object or mistaken something perfectly ordinary for a spacecraft.

David protested that dozens of other people had witnessed the same thing, but his father refused to entertain the possibility that an enormous flying saucer had been hovering above Birkenhead.

Then David's mother returned from a shopping trip.

She had barely entered the house before mentioning the extraordinary stories she had heard while she was out. Several people had told her about a gigantic flying saucer which had apparently remained suspended above Grange Road that very morning.

David immediately turned to his father. 'There you are, Dad! We can't all have been seeing things!'

But his father remained unconvinced.

He blamed television, declaring that all those daft programmes about flying saucers and visitors from outer space were putting ridiculous ideas into the heads of weak-minded people.

And that was the end of the discussion, as far as David's father was concerned.

Yet David never forgot the enormous, silent machine hanging over Grange Road, or the strange, snake-like instrument that appeared to be studying the people below.

If the many witnesses were telling the truth, what exactly had visited Birkenhead on that autumn morning in 1967?

And, perhaps more disturbingly, what had it been looking for?

Birkenhead is certainly no stranger to UFO mysteries. On Tuesday, 17 July 1962, at around 11.25 pm, a strange aerial object was reportedly seen by several people in different parts of Birkenhead.

What began as a series of sightings of an enormous flying saucer was to culminate in a disturbing incident involving three elderly vagrants who appeared to vanish without a trace.

One of the first witnesses was a 70-year-old man named Terry, who lived with his wife Mary on Argyle Street South.

That warm summer night, Terry had been studying the full moon through a pair of 10x50 Hartmann binoculars, which he had purchased from Curry & Paxton in Liverpool for £37 and 13 shillings, payable over eight months.

Mary was sitting up in bed, engrossed in an Agatha Christie novel, when she noticed her husband staring intently through the binoculars.

'I hope you're not spying on any young women, Terry,' she remarked.

'Only Diana, love,' he replied mischievously.

Mary immediately demanded to know who Diana was, and Terry explained that Diana was the Roman goddess associated with the Moon.

His wife was not amused, but a few moments later, Terry's joking manner abruptly changed.

'Mary, come here and look at this!' he exclaimed.

Mary was reluctant to abandon her book, but Terry became so excited that he shouted at her to get out of bed and see what he had discovered.

When Mary finally approached the window, she noticed that the Moon had disappeared behind what she initially assumed was a passing cloud. However, the object obscuring the lunar disc was no cloud. It was an immense, dark, circular craft moving silently across the heavens.

Terry was convinced that he was looking at a flying saucer, although he could offer no explanation for its extraordinary size or appearance.

At approximately the same time, a married couple in their thirties, Brian and Sheila, were watching the television crime series Interpol Calling at their home on Hollybank Road, Tranmere.

Sheila happened to glance towards the living-room window and noticed an unusual blue light moving beyond the net curtains. She drew Brian's attention to it, and he immediately rose from the sofa and pulled the curtains aside.

Both watched in astonishment as an enormous, luminous, disc-shaped object travelled northwards before apparently coming to a complete standstill somewhere above Hamilton Square.

Brian jokingly announced that they were witnessing a genuine flying saucer, but Sheila found nothing amusing about the spectacle.

There was something deeply menacing about the mysterious object, and she wondered what its occupants, assuming there were any, might be doing above Birkenhead.

Several minutes later, someone knocked loudly at the front door. It was their neighbour, Clive, who was eager to know whether they had seen the strange object.

Clive explained that his sister, who lived on Hampden Road, had just telephoned him to report a similar sighting. According to her, the glowing craft had approached from the direction of Rock Ferry.

'Do you think we're being invaded?' Sheila asked nervously.

Clive shrugged and replied that he sincerely hoped not, as he and his wife had only just arranged a holiday in St Tudy, Cornwall.

Brian invited Clive inside, and the three went upstairs to obtain a better view of the sky. Unfortunately, the mysterious object was nowhere to be seen.

However, according to other accounts of the incident, the craft had not departed. Its brilliant blue illumination had simply been extinguished, leaving its dark outline almost indistinguishable against the night sky.

Meanwhile, another couple were enjoying what should have been one of the happiest evenings of their lives.

Barbara, a beautiful blonde bus conductress aged 21, was walking along Grange Road with her boyfriend, Rob, a 24-year-old television repairman from Tees Street.

The couple had been courting for only two months, but earlier that evening, during a visit to the Glass Barrel Hotel on Market Street, Rob had unexpectedly proposed marriage. Barbara had delightedly accepted.

The newly engaged couple had subsequently visited several public houses and were now making their way towards a fish-and-chip shop. Afterwards, Rob intended to escort his fiancée home to Priory Buildings.

As they walked along Grange Road, they encountered three elderly vagrants, one of whom removed his battered trilby and politely approached Rob.

The man explained that neither he nor his two companions had eaten for three days and asked whether the young gentleman could spare a little money.

Rob, still elated by Barbara's acceptance of his proposal, reached into his trouser pocket and produced a ten-shilling note and a handful of pennies.

He cheerfully handed the money to the elderly stranger, who thanked him profusely, revealing a broad, toothless grin.

'You'll have good luck for that, young man,' the vagrant assured him, before wishing the couple goodnight.

The three men then continued along Grange Road, leaving Rob and Barbara to resume their journey.

They had almost reached the chip shop when Rob became aware of something peculiar overhead.

A vast, dark shape was moving slowly across the sky, blotting out the stars as it passed. Its outline appeared elliptical, and Rob could scarcely believe the size of the object.

He stopped walking and pointed upwards, urging Barbara to look.

Barbara, who was a little merry after the evening's celebrations, initially misunderstood what had attracted his attention. She gazed affectionately at Rob and remarked upon the romantic beauty of the moonlit night.

But Rob was no longer listening. He continued staring at the enormous black object, trying to determine what it could possibly be.

Then, without warning, the mysterious craft became illuminated by an intense, steady blue light.

Barbara looked up and gasped.

The object was unmistakably a gigantic flying saucer, and Rob estimated that it measured at least 500 feet across.

Before either could fully comprehend what they were witnessing, something even more extraordinary happened.

A powerful shaft of dazzling light suddenly emerged from the underside of the craft and descended towards Grange Road.

The beam settled directly upon the three elderly vagrants whom Rob had helped only minutes earlier.

Barbara screamed. Both she and Rob believed they could hear the distant cries of the three men as they stood enveloped in the unearthly brilliance.

Then, as abruptly as it had appeared, the beam was switched off. The three vagrants had vanished.

Rob and Barbara stared in disbelief at the spot where the men had been standing. There was no sign of them anywhere.

Other pedestrians had also noticed the gigantic object and stopped to watch it in astonishment.

The saucer's blue illumination gradually faded, and the enormous craft began ascending into the night sky. It continued climbing until it finally disappeared from sight. The fate of the three elderly men remains the most disturbing aspect of this extraordinary account. Had they somehow escaped the beam and hurried away, or had something far more sinister occurred?

Years later, when I recounted the incident during a local radio broadcast, the programme received a flood of telephone calls from listeners. Yet despite the interest generated by the story, I was never able to establish the identities of the three vagrants, nor could I discover whether any of them had ever been seen again.

And so, more than six decades after that strange July night, the alleged disappearance of three unfortunate men beneath a mysterious blue light remains one of Birkenhead's most unsettling UFO mysteries.

* Tom Slemen's latest book, 100 Scary Tales, is out now on Amazon.
